title: Third distinction: honor proprie vs improprie—legate, funeral statue; from Bellarmine
source_text: XXXVIII. Tertio notant posse aliquid honorari proprie, vel improprie. Id, ut aiunt, proprie dicitur honorari, quod vere ratione sui ipsius honoratur. Improprie dicitur honorari, quod honoratur loco alterius. Legatus Regis aliquando honoratur ut legatus, & tunc ipse proprie honoratur, licet propter alium honoretur: aliquando honoratur loco Regis, honore proprio Regibus, & tunc ipse improprie honoratur, proprie autem Rex in ipso tunc honoratur. Id clarius apparet cum funus celebratur absente corpore, circa statuam, & fiunt erga statuam omnia quae circa corpus fierent, &c. Quae distinctiones omnes sunt Bellarmini libro secundo de Ecclesia triumphante capite vigesimo.
pass_a_gloss: Thirdly they note that something can be honored properly, or improperly. That, as they say, is said to be honored properly which is truly honored by reason of itself. That is said to be honored improperly which is honored in place of another. A King's legate is sometimes honored as legate, and then he himself is properly honored, though he is honored on account of another; sometimes he is honored in place of the King, with the honor proper to Kings, and then he himself is improperly honored, but the King is properly honored in him. That appears more clearly when a funeral is celebrated with the body absent, around a statue, and everything is done toward the statue that would be done around the body, and so on. All which distinctions are Bellarmine's, in the second book On the Triumphant Church, chapter twenty.
pass_b_english: Third cut: proper vs improper honor.
Proper: honored by reason of itself; improper: honored in another's place — legate for the king; funeral statue for the corpse.
Bellarmine, De Ecclesia triumphante II.20, is the source for all three distinctions.

choices.why: Stock School example for improper honor.
